articles.title: FX Outlook 2027: Seven key calls
articles.author: Chris Turner, Francesco Pesole, Frantisek Taborsky, Deepali Bhargava
articles.fulltext:
We expect 2027 to be a low-volatility year in FX, with central banks and rate differentials firmly in the driving seat. We see a dollar decline resuming from 2Q27, while diverging monetary, growth and external dynamics create opportunities across regions
Winners and losers in FX next year
Not a breakout year for volatility
Our most important FX call for 2027 is the market environment. Our macro-driven call is that lower oil prices and only a modest recalibration in global monetary policy mean that FX volatility can stay low. This is not 2022/2023, when major central banks belatedly delivered 500bp tightening cycles to deal with double-digit inflation. If 2026 has shown us anything, it is that FX markets can prove quite resilient in this high-growth, high-inflation global economy. And markets have proved quite resilient to geopolitical risk as well.
For the majority of the last five years, the market has overestimated FX volatility. There may be some structural factors at play here, such as huge growth in financial assets bringing in more liquidity to the FX market and the greater use of FX pricing algos on the buy-side, limiting the market fallout when trading conditions thin.
Yet market volatility has not vanished. There are plenty of risks out there, which we highlight in a dedicated section below. The same applies for market liquidity. If the shock is big enough – such as Liberation Day tariffs in 2025 or the start of the Iran war this year – market depth can fall away quickly. The prospect of fat tails, low-probability, high-impact event risks, is certainly a threat to global FX markets. But the bar for these risks to raise volatility is a high one.
Volatility has mostly undershot expectations in 2026
Look no further than central banks in G10
In a year dominated by geopolitical risk and energy shock, currency investors quickly moved beyond headline trading and increasingly looked to short-term rate differentials as the primary guide for currencies. We expect that to remain the case next year.
Central bank tightening is moving beyond its “insurance” phase, requiring evidence that inflationary pressures are becoming persistent. Oil prices will remain part of the story, but we think the more important distinction is between economies where the shock can generate more lasting inflation and those where it cannot. On top of that, the central banks’ FX-specific approach will be key. Remember how, in 2022-2024, the fear of amplified inflation effects from a weak currency prompted tighter fiscal policies among some often dovish-leaning central banks.
Here are our top picks among G10 currencies for next year:
JPY – the best risk/reward. We don’t have a huge outperformance of the yen in our forecasts, especially relative to the euro. But that’s primarily due to our assumption that the euro will drop its French-related risk premium by end-2028, and a carry-favourable environment can somewhat contain yen gains. However, we think the yen offers the best risk-reward profile in G10. Alongside being sharply undervalued based on long-term fundamentals, it faces limited risks of dovish repricing as the Bank of Japan’s tightening cycle predated the Iran war. It incidentally has strong safe-haven value against some fat-tail risks (AI bust, fiscal dominance, dollar debasement, some geopolitical events) and stands to be a beneficiary of an ultimate capitulation in USD rates. Downside risks are, crucially, limited by a coordinated Tokyo-Washington effort to prevent sharp USD/JPY rallies.
CHF – SNB turning pro-franc . If 2027 is the year when global interest rates peak and then reverse, the opportunity cost of holding the franc starts to fall. We also think the Swiss National Bank will prove more tolerant of franc strength. Not only are there fewer complaints about the strong franc from local corporates, but Switzerland’s inflation is much lower than trading partners and the SNB might again opt for nominal franc appreciation to keep the real exchange rate stable.
NZD – The high-beta gamble. Among higher-beta currencies, we see good potential for the New Zealand dollar next year. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has delivered a few dovish surprises, but we think it is underestimating the inflation risks for 2027: we expect at least two hikes, also helped by a fairly robust growth backdrop. NZD should be favoured against the Australian dollar to play a decline in global rates, as the Reserve Bank of Australia may already shift to cuts in the third quarter of 2027.
Sterling, dollar and AUD face largest dovish repricing risk
Dollar decline is delayed, not cancelled
Our baseline for global inflation in 2027 remains benign, leaving most of our major central bank calls more dovish than current market pricing. We expect the Federal Reserve to deliver one final hike in December 2026, taking rates to a 4.25% peak, but we don’t think the additional hikes priced by 3Q27 will materialise. Modest second-round effects should fail to sustain inflation once the 2Q27 base-effect decline comes through. Importantly, and unlike in other economies, we think benign inflation rather than weaker growth will be the main catalyst for a dovish Fed turn. That means markets may be reluctant to price a large Fed cutting cycle too early, but it’s equally an environment where we envision a Fed cut in 4Q27. Ultimately, we expect a nearly 100bp drop in the 2-year USD swap rate by the end of 2027, with most of the move concentrated in the year’s second half.
We expect the dollar to weaken alongside that repricing, with greater conviction in the downside story later in the year. The Fed should remain cautious about turning dovish before clearer evidence of disinflation emerges, while elevated funding rates will continue to make it expensive to sell or hedge dollars until some easing is priced in. And because we also hold dovish views on other central banks, we don’t expect narrower USD short-term rate differentials to trigger a particularly large dollar downturn. We target a roughly 5% decline in DXY to 97 by end-2027.
Front-end rates to drive DXY lower
Bond premium on the euro needs bad news fuel
Our colleagues in the macro and rates team remain cautious about a recovery in French sentiment in the next couple of quarters. Weak growth (0.5% in 2027) should continue to make fiscal arithmetic complicated, and we forecast a deficit of 5.5% next year – assuming a budget is passed – above the 5.0% government target. Election frontrunner Marine Le Pen has signalled large spending cuts, although their credibility remains in question . She is, anyway, a more market-friendly candidate than left-wing rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
We think markets will be wary of jumping into a meaningful OAT relief rally before the presidential election (18 April-2 May) and likely parliamentary elections in the summer are out of the way. We are not forecasting another big selloff in French bonds but think 125-150bp will be the norm for the OAT-Bund 10yr spread into 2Q27, before some tightening towards 100bp in 2H27.
The euro has been embedding a French risk premium since early October, meaning a further material deterioration in sentiment would probably be needed to generate additional idiosyncratic pressure. Historically, the link between euro-area sovereign spreads and FX has been patchy, with stress episodes often requiring a steady flow of negative news to sustain the correlation.
We therefore expect French political risk to keep euro sentiment somewhat subdued into the elections and a subsequent bond-market relief rally to offer some support, but not to displace central bank expectations as the main driver of EUR crosses next year. In other words, we really need to see a significant deterioration in the French situation, prompting ECB bond market intervention, for EUR/USD to sustain a move below 1.10 through 2027.
EUR already embeds French risk premium
Central Europe: Same shocks, different paths for local FX
The Central Europe region is entering a year of divergence. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary face similar risks from energy prices, geopolitics and volatile global markets, but increasingly different monetary, fiscal and growth dynamics mean CEE3 is becoming less of a single FX trade.
In the Czech Republic, the Czech National Bank has already delivered two hikes, taking rates to 4%, and remains the most hawkish central bank in the region. If inflation proves more persistent, further tightening remains possible. Positive nominal and real rate differentials and high credibility should therefore keep the koruna relatively defensive during periods of global uncertainty, while any easing of external risks could put it back on an appreciation path.
Poland is moving differently. The National Bank of Poland is still waiting to deliver its first hike, leaving the zloty with less monetary support for now. Strong growth and sizeable EU inflows remain important anchors, but narrower rate differentials, loose fiscal policy and rising political and rating risks have weakened PLN’s relative appeal. We therefore see the zloty as more vulnerable to higher global yields, energy prices and geopolitical risks.
Hungary is heading in the opposite direction, with the National Bank of Hungary having cut rates in recent months. We expect another cut only later next year, provided global conditions allow it. Attractive carry, EU-fund inflows and an improving external balance should support the forint, while progress towards euro adoption provides another positive longer-term story. The central bank’s focus on the exchange rate should meanwhile limit the pace of easing and keep EUR/HUF biased towards the stronger end of its range.
Divergent central bank responses to the same shock (%)
Asia: Rotation underway, tech currencies should lead
A softer dollar should provide a broad tailwind for Asian FX, particularly in the second half of 2027, but we expect performance to remain highly differentiated. We favour the Korean won and Taiwanese dollar, expect further renminbi appreciation – albeit with greater two-way volatility – and see continued downside risks for the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso. We are more constructive on the Indian rupee.
Current account strength should continue to favour the tech currencies. Although the AI cycle may be plateauing, activity remains high and strong export revenues should support the KRW and TWD. Exporter FX conversion and measures encouraging the repatriation of overseas assets should provide additional support. CNY should also benefit from strong external balances, although we expect a less one-directional appreciation trend.
Rate support will become less favourable. Most Asian central banks are further advanced in their tightening cycles than the Fed and should finish hiking by early 2027 before preparing for easing. Narrowing rate support should particularly weigh on the rate-sensitive IDR. Continued household and corporate demand for foreign assets could also offset some of the benefits from strong current accounts.
Lower oil and food prices should help importers in the second half of 2027, but capital flows are unlikely to recover evenly. Political uncertainty and the MSCI downgrade should also remain headwinds for the IDR, while weaker FDI inflows leave the PHP vulnerable. By contrast, we favour the INR, where resilient growth, supply-chain diversification and continued FDI should provide support, while leaving India less exposed to swings in the AI cycle.
Asia: change in current account balance and local currency (2Q26 vs 2Q25)
Latam: Banxico’s neglect of the peso stands out
We’ve said that central bank policy is going to be more important than ever in 2027. And exchange rates can be an important part of the monetary toolkit – especially in small, open economies. In a world where central bank tightening cycles are being priced more hawkishly, Banxico’s unabashedly dovish stance stands out.
When cutting rates to 6.25% in November, Banxico noted that, because of slack economic conditions, the pass-through of exchange rate fluctuations to consumer prices would be limited. The IMF puts that economic ‘slack’ – or the negative output gap – at 0.4% of GDP in 2027. That makes Banxico far less concerned about a weaker currency than most other central banks.
In addition, Banxico has now cut the peso’s policy rate protection to just 225bp over the Fed. That is a record low and leaves the peso vulnerable to any deterioration in the external environment. We see the peso as a relative underperformer in 2027.
Further south, the Brazilian real has been causing a lot of pain to investors recently. The fear is that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s pre-election giveaways will come home to roost next year. His choice of Finance Minister is going to be important, as will any progress on a 2027 budget. Preventing a bigger sell-off in the real, however, is the independent central bank running very high real interest rates. It’s a courageous call, but we think the real can recover a lot of its recent losses and outperform Mexico’s peso.

articles.title: Asia FX Outlook 2027: Rotation underway but tech currencies should lead
articles.author: Deepali Bhargava, Lynn Song, Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
The recent sell-off in oil prices has provided some much-needed relief to South Asian currencies. Looking into 2027, and assuming the dollar does start to soften, we prefer to back the tech-linked currencies of North Asia. These currencies are backed by large current account surpluses – surpluses which could be coming home
Executive summary
Asian currencies have had a mixed run in 2026. AI export-linked currencies (the Korean won, Chinese yuan, Singapore dollar, and Malaysian ringgit) generally outperformed, while less direct beneficiaries such as the Indian rupee, Indonesian rupiah, and Philippine peso each weakened by more than 5%. Deteriorating political dynamics and supply-side shocks from higher energy prices further weighed on growth prospects and added pressure on these currencies. One notable exception among the tech-linked economies was the Taiwanese dollar, which depreciated by around 5% despite strong current account balances, as a tech-sector sell-off in recent months triggered equity outflows. In contrast, the Singapore dollar delivered another year of strong gains, supported by AI-related exports and stronger-than-expected economic growth.
Post-midterms, there has been a rotation from North Asian to South Asian currencies, driven by the tech sell-off and lower oil prices, which have helped improve valuations in parts of South Asia. Looking ahead, a softer dollar should provide a tailwind for Asian FX in 2027. However, we see further downside risks for the PHP and IDR given persistent external vulnerabilities and weaker capital inflows, while tech-linked currencies such as the KRW and CNY are likely to outperform as current account surpluses likely play a larger role in driving performance. CNY appreciation should continue, but with greater two-way volatility.
Still -strong current account support for tech currencies: We remain bullish on the KRW and TWD. In our view, the AI cycle may be plateauing, but activity remains at a high level. Strong AI-related exports should continue to support current account balances, while exporter FX conversion should help offset capital outflows. In addition, new measures to encourage the repatriation of overseas assets could provide further support for both currencies.
Rate differentials and resident outflows are becoming less supportive for EM Asia: Most Asian central banks are further ahead in their tightening cycles than the Fed. We expect most to complete their hiking cycles by the first quarter of 2027 and begin preparing for policy easing thereafter. As a result, interest rate support for Asian currencies is likely to diminish and negatively impact rate-sensitive currencies like IDR the most. At the same time, households and corporates continue to favour foreign currency assets, reflecting still-elevated global yields and a desire to diversify savings away from domestic currencies. This preference for foreign assets could offset some of the support from strong current account balances and limit the upside for Asian FX, even as the broader dollar outlook becomes more favourable.
Oil and food price risks should largely be behind us by the second half of 2027. This should benefit oil-importing currencies such as the PHP, IDR and INR. However, tighter global financial conditions mean capital inflows are unlikely to be distributed evenly. Political uncertainty and the MSCI downgrade will continue to weigh on investor sentiment towards IDR, while weaker FDI inflows remain a challenge for PHP. We remain more constructive on the INR, where growth should stay relatively more resilient, supported by supply chain diversification, continued FDI inflows, and lower vulnerability to swings in the AI cycle.
Currency sections
USD/CNY: Steady appreciation trend to face two-way risks ahead
PBoC has overseen a smooth period of continuous moderate CNY appreciation: USD/CNY has been on a steady downward trend over the past year and has been one of the surprising outperformers amid a strong dollar backdrop. We currently pencil in one 10bp rate cut from the People’s Bank of China (PBoC) next year, along with further targeted easing measures. Eventually, the interest rate spread should attract some CNY bears into action. The PBoC’s stance could shift after being supportive of further strengthening over the past year. We see some signs of pushback against appreciation already; in an October policy statement, the PBoC warned against one-sided and pro-cyclical behaviour in the FX market, and in November, it hiked the foreign-exchange deposit reserve requirement from 4% to 6%. If the PBoC pushes back more strongly, it could well mark the end of the CNY appreciation cycle.
CNY headwinds should remain on the radar: US-China yield spreads widened to the highest levels in decades in 2026, and short-term spreads could widen further as the Fed has started rate hikes, while the PBoC is still easing policy. Growth is expected to be more stable in 2027 after a year of moderation in 2026. This year was also an unusually weak year for outbound investment, as we saw the introduction of tighter rules on outward direct investment, leading to a surprise contraction of outward direct investment (ODI) after years of solid growth. Similarly, a crackdown on overseas investment income may have discouraged further outflows. If outbound investment normalises in 2027, this could be a catalyst for a USD/CNY rebound.
Base case is for continued appreciation, but the path may not be so smooth next year: Considering the foreign currency left overseas in recent years, and with incoming foreign currency receivables with China’s trade surplus set to hit a new record high in 2026, the stage is set for further CNY appreciation. At this point, this view is widely accepted, which in the near-term helps reinforce the trend, but also raises the question of whether most market participants are already fully positioned in this direction. While the CNY will remain a relatively low-volatility currency, we don’t expect the straight-line appreciation of the past year to continue for another year. We set an initial fluctuation band forecast of 6.40-6.80 for 2027, with a 2027 year-end forecast of 6.50. Two-way fluctuation looks likely to return, and a strong CNY appreciation bias in markets raises the risks for a stronger reversal.
USD/IDR: Renewed weakening pressures likely for the IDR
Growth continued to surprise on the upside through the first three quarters of 2026, with GDP expanding well above expectations. Both domestic and external demand contributed to the strong performance. Exports remained supported by robust demand for manufactured goods, while domestically, investment activity and household consumption held up despite rising political uncertainty and persistent capital outflows. Government spending accelerated and capital expenditure remained strong, reflecting confidence in Indonesia's medium-term growth prospects. Fiscal deficit targets were raised but remain below the legislative cap of 3%. Importantly, stronger growth has not come at the expense of price stability, with inflation remaining well contained, supported in part by government subsidies. However, this macroeconomic resilience has yet to translate into higher investor confidence and capital inflows, which is keeping IDR under pressure. As a result, we expect Bank Indonesia (BI) to hike by 25bp in December, with the last hike this cycle being delivered in 1Q27.
Political uncertainty and MSCI downgrade: Indonesian assets have come under significant pressure this year, with the rupiah among Asia's weakest currencies and the Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) down more than 42% year-to-date, making it one of the region's worst-performing equity markets. Investor sentiment has been weighed down by rising policy uncertainty under the Prabowo administration, concerns over energy subsidies, and questions around the implementation of structural reforms. These concerns have intensified following MSCI's review of Indonesia's market classification, with a potential downgrade from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status. The decision is expected by mid-2027, raising the risk of sustained portfolio outflows. MSCI's concerns centre on market accessibility issues, including opaque shareholding structures, suspected coordinated trading activity, and insufficient evidence of regulatory enforcement. If the downgrade is announced, it could trigger billions of US dollars in foreign outflows from Indonesia markets.
Indonesia's external position has deteriorated , with the current account deficit widening to $3.5bn in 2Q26 from near balance at the end of 2025, and pressures are likely to intensify. Slowing export growth has reduced support from the trade balance, while FDI inflows weakened further in 1H26. As a result, Indonesia recorded a balance of payments deficit of $10bn in 1H26, the largest on record, highlighting growing strains in the country's external accounts. At the same time, foreign investors remain cautious amid concerns over fiscal slippage, as higher oil prices and El Niño-related subsidy spending weigh on the fiscal outlook. We therefore continue to see downside risks to the rupiah. Narrowing rate differentials as BI nears the end of its rate hikes and widening external deficit inflows leave the currency increasingly vulnerable. With FX reserves no longer rising meaningfully, Bank Indonesia's ability to smooth sustained depreciation pressures may become more constrained over time.
USD/INR: Downside risks for INR likely to be diminished
The RBI delivered its first rate hike in four years, raised its growth and inflation forecasts, and signalled a path of gradual policy normalisation. While the tone was hawkish, the message was one of calibrated tightening rather than an aggressive hiking cycle. Rate cuts are firmly off the table, but the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also appears reluctant to tighten liquidity sharply or front-load rate hikes. Barring a material inflation surprise from persistently high oil prices, a stronger-than-expected El Niño impact on food prices, or a sharper INR depreciation, we expect the RBI to continue tightening gradually. Our base case is for a further 50bp of hikes over the next six months, taking the repo rate to 6.0%. With inflation projected at 5.2% in FY27, this would lift the real repo rate to around 50bp, returning policy to positive real rate territory but still below the RBI's longer-term comfort level of around 1%, suggesting scope for further normalisation should inflation risks materialise.
India remains in a relative sweet spot: Growth has remained resilient through 2026, supported by robust domestic demand and a stronger external backdrop. Export growth has held up well as firms continue to diversify export destinations, while easing tariff-related tensions with the US and the new trade agreement with the EU have supported a reorientation towards European markets, where export momentum has strengthened. As a result, manufacturing activity has remained robust whereas investment growth has been underpinned by strong government spending. While India benefited less from the AI-driven export boom than North Asian economies, it is also less exposed to a potential correction as the cycle matures. Structural reforms, ongoing infrastructure investment, and resilient services exports should leave India well positioned to outperform many regional peers as the AI cycle normalises.
Downside risks have diminished: India’s external position has weakened, with the current account deficit projected to widen to 2.5% of GDP in 2026 from 0.7% in 2025. While RBI measures to attract foreign inflows helped support the balance of payments, frequent policy adjustments have raised some concerns about policy consistency. The more significant headwinds, however, have come from higher oil prices and India’s relatively limited participation in the AI-driven export boom. Looking ahead, lower oil-related risk premia should improve India’s terms of trade and reduce pressure on the INR, while the decline in oil prices has encouraged a recovery in foreign portfolio inflows. Nevertheless, reserve adequacy has declined recently following foreign outflows from equity markets and recent FX intervention, and the RBI is likely to use periods of INR strength to rebuild reserves. So, while downside risks to INR have diminished, the scope for sustained appreciation remains limited, leaving the currency broadly stable rather than materially stronger.
USD/KRW: Offshore money comes home
Domestic demand picks up, BOK stays hawkish: Korea seemingly has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom this year. Having expected the Korean economy to grow by 1.8% at the start of the year, the Bank of Korea (BOK) now expects GDP growth in excess of 3.3% this year and above 2.9% in 2027. Encouragingly, strong exports and investment are broadening into consumption at a time of cyclically low unemployment (2.6%). In response, the Bank has hiked the policy rate twice to 3.00% and is considering further tightening. Money markets price a move close to 3.50%, which was the peak of the cycle back in 2023, when inflation was running above 6%. That looks like the direction of travel for the policy rate, though the central bank remains worried about surging house prices and high levels of household debt.
A U-turn in sentiment: Having traded as high as 1,550 in June, the subsequent drop in USD/KRW to 1,350 has been eye-watering. Driving that has been a turnaround in portfolio flows. In May and June, foreigners sold around $30bn of Korean assets each month. Those outflows have since slowed. Clearly, the performance of Samsung and SK Hynix, which together comprise around 50% of the Kospi index, is going to have a big say here. But our house view of the AI story plateauing at a high level suggests it is too early to call the Kospi a big negative for the won. In any case, the correlation between the won and the Kospi regularly flips from positive to negative and is hard to rely on. Instead, we think government measures to encourage greater repatriation of FX export proceeds have been a bigger driver of won gains recently.
Stronger growth can see more repatriation: We expect Korea’s 15-20% current account surplus to play a more meaningful role in driving won gains in 2027. Korea’s current account surplus is close to $50bn per month and the challenge for Korean authorities is to get exporters to bring that money home. Overseas reinvested earnings did see a big drop in response to government measures in 2023. Since then, the story has been mixed. But in 2027, we think a combination of higher domestic growth rates, higher interest rates and new incentives (tax breaks, etc.) can see more export earnings chase opportunities in Korea. Looking at Korea’s real, trade-weighted exchange rate, we see it around 5% below its 10-year average. A return to average levels would put USD/KRW somewhere near 1,275, which is our call for the end of 2027.
USD/PHP: FX fundamentals remain challenging for PHP
Inflation in the Philippines remains the highest in the region , averaging 5.5% year-on-year in January to October 2026, with the latest reading accelerating to 7.8% YoY, driven largely by higher fuel prices and their pass-through into core inflation. The BSP's 50bp jumbo hike in October was likely delivered in anticipation of this inflation surge. Looking ahead, easing oil prices, a weaker USD and uncertainty surrounding developments in Iran following the US midterm elections suggest that Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) may prefer to assess the cumulative impact of past tightening rather than move aggressively again. If oil prices continue to decline and 3Q GDP growth disappoints, the case for another jumbo hike appears limited. Nevertheless, we maintain our base case for a final 25bp rate hike in December, taking the policy rate to 5.75%. While the inflation outlook is improving, core inflation remains sticky, and the BSP is likely to retain a cautious tightening bias to keep inflation expectations anchored and stay ahead of potential upside risks.
Growth is likely to strengthen and recover to 5.0% in 2027 , following a weaker-than-expected first half of 2026 that was weighed down by fiscal underperformance. As government spending normalises, favourable base effects kick in, and lower energy prices support household purchasing power, both business and consumer activity should improve. Labour market conditions have softened, with unemployment rising alongside weaker demand in government capex. Wage growth in construction and services has lagged inflation, constraining household incomes. The bright spot remains the manufacturing sector, where wages have held up better, rising nearly 8.5% YoY in the first half of the year. Labour demand in manufacturing also remains robust, with job postings up almost 30% YoY, suggesting continued strength in export-oriented and industrial sectors. Overall, the growth outlook is poised to improve, although risks remain tilted to the downside due to ongoing political uncertainty and potential spillovers from Middle East tensions.
FX fundamentals remain challenging, pointing to continued currency weakness: Narrow rate differentials and a widening current account deficit continue to weigh on the peso, while the BSP has drawn on its foreign exchange reserves to smooth currency volatility. As a result, reserve adequacy has deteriorated, with import cover declining to around 6.2 months, the lowest level since 2018. While the weaker peso has provided a boost to electronics exports and improved export competitiveness, this has not been sufficient to prevent a significant widening in the current account deficit. Strong import demand, particularly for capital and intermediate goods, has more than offset export gains. Services exports and remittance inflows remain resilient, but foreign direct investment inflows have weakened considerably, reducing a key source of stable external financing. Taken together, the balance of payments outlook remains soft, suggesting limited scope for sustained currency appreciation despite an improving growth backdrop.
USD/SGD: Another year of relative strength for SGD
Still-vigilant MAS: While the inflation outlook has improved following the recent correction in oil prices, risks have not disappeared. Domestic inflation could prove stickier if spillovers from the AI-driven investment cycle become more broad-based, boosting demand and pushing labour costs higher than expected. Weather-related disruptions, including El Niño-related risks, could also add to food price pressures. As such, we continue to see the balance of inflation risks as modestly skewed to the upside in the near term, even though inflation is likely to begin moderating from mid-2027 after these risks subside. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is likely to remain vigilant, closely monitoring developments in energy prices, food inflation and domestic demand conditions. Any renewed rise in domestic inflation pressures could prompt a further tightening move in the January policy review.
Strong growth performance: Singapore’s GDP growth averaged 6% YoY in the first three quarters, far exceeding expectations and highlighting the economy's resilience. The economy has benefited disproportionately from the global AI investment cycle, which has boosted demand for semiconductors, electronics and other high-value manufacturing exports. At the same time, domestic demand has remained firm, supported by a tight labour market, healthy wage growth and solid credit expansion. Looking ahead, we expect growth to moderate as the pace of AI-related investment and export growth normalises from exceptionally strong levels. Nevertheless, GDP growth is still projected to remain at a robust 4.0% YoY in 2027, above its long-run trend. Continued strength in domestic demand, ongoing investments in advanced manufacturing capacity and Singapore's central role in AI-related supply chains should help sustain growth even as external tailwinds become less pronounced.
Strong external balance sheet should support SGD: The SGD nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) is trading near the top of its policy band, around 1.6% above the midpoint of the ±2% band, limiting the scope for further policy-driven appreciation. Even so, we expect the Singapore dollar to outperform most regional currencies. Resilient growth, supported by AI-related exports, strong manufacturing activity and firm domestic demand, should continue to attract capital inflows. Singapore has also emerged as one of the region's largest beneficiaries of supply chain diversification and geopolitical fragmentation, capturing roughly a quarter of Asia's net FDI inflows since the pandemic as it positions itself as a neutral hub that attracts investment from both US and Chinese firms. In addition, USD/SGD remains closely correlated with DXY and should benefit from further US dollar weakness. Together, resilient growth, sustained capital inflows, supportive monetary policy expectations and a softer US dollar should keep the Singapore dollar well supported relative to its regional peers.
USD/TWD: AI trajectory could determine TWD direction
Hedging changes, outbound investment, and the central bank stance have been TWD headwinds: At the start of 2026, Taiwanese life insurers were able to apply an FX-amortisation method to directly held foreign-currency debt securities classified at amortised cost, reducing the incentive to hedge and with TWD forward buying falling as a result. Outbound investment was also a major consideration, as we’ve seen the US-Taiwan yield spread widen significantly through the year. Taiwanese corporates have also raised overseas investment amid aggressive capacity expansion. The Central Bank of the Republic of China (CBC) has decided to hold rates steady so far after a round of global central bank tightening. Although we expect a rate hike in December, the CBC has been less hawkish than most global peers, and this should continue as we expect the December move may be one-and-done. The CBC has also played a role in limiting TWD movement via interventions.
Taiwan has been one of the world’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, but the TWD hasn’t shown it: This year, Taiwan has managed double-digit GDP growth in the first three quarters, and we have seen Taiwan’s trade surplus over the first 10 months of the year rise 57.7% YoY to US$188.5bn, breaking a new record high. At the same time, AI optimism also led the TAIEX to reach a record high in October and attracted significant foreign capital inflows until the recent selloff. Despite this seemingly positive combination, USD/TWD has traded within a range of 31.2-33.0 through 2026, with the TWD weakening overall against the USD since the start of the year.
Heading into 2027, AI industry developments will likely remain the main driver for the TWD, which could stage a recovery in 2027: On the current account side, we expect that full order books for Taiwan’s leading tech companies, driven by AI capex, will result in continued strong trade growth in the year ahead, and exporter repatriation should eventually play a larger role in the TWD trajectory. While the factors leading to TWD depreciation this year remain a consideration, these headwinds are likely already well reflected in the current level for the TWD. As such, we see risks being balanced toward a moderate recovery next year, where we have the TWD strengthening to 31.5 by the end of 2027.

articles.title: EMEA FX Outlook 2027: Restrictive policy remains the key FX anchor
articles.author: Chris Turner, Rafal Benecki, Adam Antoniak, Mateusz Sutowicz, Peter Virovacz, David Havrlant, Dmitry Dolgin, Valentin Tataru, Stefan Posea, Muhammet Mercan, Frantisek Taborsky
articles.fulltext:
EMEA FX should remain supported by restrictive policy and attractive carry, but performance will increasingly diverge. We favour HUF, ZAR and TRY, while CZK remains supported and PLN faces headwinds. Global yields, energy prices, fiscal risks and geopolitics remain key drivers
Executive summary
Central banks across EMEA remain focused on currency stability as inflation, fiscal risks and geopolitics keep the external environment challenging. Restrictive monetary policy and attractive carry support several currencies, particularly the forint, rand and lira, while solid external balances and EU inflows provide additional buffers. At the same time, high global yields, energy price risks, fiscal concerns and geopolitical uncertainty should drive greater differentiation across the region.
The CEE3 region, comprising the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland, should remain relatively well supported by restrictive monetary policy, although the outlook is becoming more differentiated. The Hungarian forint remains our preferred Central European currency, with the National Bank of Hungary expected to keep rates at 5.50% for the next 9-12 months, while fiscal consolidation, EU-fund inflows and an improving external balance should keep the forint biased towards the stronger end of its 350-370 EUR/HUF range. The Czech koruna should also benefit from positive nominal and real rate differentials after the Czech National Bank raised rates to 4%, although weaker growth should prevent a renewed hiking cycle. By contrast, we have turned mildly negative on the Polish zloty. Narrower rate differentials, fiscal concerns and rising political and rating risks should limit PLN performance, despite strong economic growth and sizeable EU inflows. Overall, global yields, energy prices and geopolitics are likely to remain important drivers across the region.
Real policy rate (%)
In the managed currency segment in EMEA, the Romanian leu should see greater stability after the volatility of the past two years. Fiscal consolidation, diminishing rating risks and lower government borrowing needs have improved Romania’s fundamental story, while weak growth and falling inflation should allow the National Bank of Romania to start cutting rates next year. However, the central bank appears more willing to tolerate FX volatility than in the past, suggesting that stability around current EUR/RON levels should not be mistaken for a return to the exceptionally tight management seen historically. Meanwhile, the Central Bank of Turkey should continue its gradual easing cycle while maintaining sufficiently attractive real rates to contain dollarisation and support reserves. Although disinflation has been delayed and inflation risks remain tilted to the upside, renewed reserve accumulation and contained FX demand suggest the current exchange-rate regime remains firmly in place. We therefore expect the lira to continue offering attractive carry despite ongoing nominal depreciation.
On the periphery of the EMEA region, South Africa’s rand should remain well supported by a hawkish central bank and attractive carry. With inflation pressures elevated, the South African Reserve Bank is keeping policy firmly restrictive, while relatively low volatility has reinforced the rand’s appeal. Progress on energy and freight reforms could provide an additional tailwind in 2027, particularly if the external environment improves, leaving the rand among the stronger performers in our EMEA forecast. Israel’s shekel faces a more balanced outlook. The Bank of Israel has responded to low inflation and excessive currency strength with rate cuts and FX intervention, signalling limited appetite for further appreciation. Softer US tech performance could also weigh on investment and hedging flows. However, Israel’s persistent current account surplus, strong reserve position and solid credit fundamentals should limit depreciation, while any improvement in geopolitics would provide renewed support.
Currency sections
EUR/PLN: Turning negative on the zloty
We are shifting our view on the zloty from neutral to mildly negative: The latest weakening of the zloty was driven mainly by global factors: a hawkish Fed, high US Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and concerns over French public finances. Rate hikes by both the Fed and the ECB have also narrowed Poland's interest rate advantage, eroding PLN’s carry appeal. Solid fundamentals should nonetheless prevent a disorderly depreciation: Poland remains one of the fastest-growing EU economies, its external position is sound, significant inflows from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) and the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence programme are still ahead, and foreign investors' exposure to Polish bonds is light. Moreover, the National Bank of Poland (NBP) may tighten monetary policy in early 2027. However, many of these factors are already priced in.
Risks to the zloty are primarily domestic and geopolitical: Several downside risks for PLN have intensified. Public finances remain the key vulnerability: the fiscal deficit is the largest in the EU, public debt is rising and approaching statutory thresholds, and no meaningful consolidation is planned before the 2027 parliamentary elections. Tense cohabitation between the government and the President limits the scope for fiscal repair, while the escalating dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal adds to the risk premium. Rating pressure is mounting, with one rating downgrade already delivered this year and the second outlook revised to negative. Geopolitically, high energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict, escalation of the war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks on Europe remain the main threats .
We expect EUR/PLN to remain in a 4.32-4.45 range over the coming months: In the near term, risks are skewed towards a weaker zloty, as a negative rating action or an escalation of domestic political tensions could push the pair towards the upper bound. A gradual recovery of the zloty in 2027 would require sustainably lower energy prices, lower global yields, a firmer stance from the NBP, and continued EU-fund inflows. Even then, loose fiscal policy ahead of the elections makes a return to the stronger levels seen in the first half of this year unlikely.
EUR/HUF: Rangebound, with a stronger-forint bias
The forint remains a prisoner of global forces: With the fiscal consolidation plan presented and preparations for the EU’s Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) II talks underway, there is no longer a single domestic event that can be circled as the next major market trigger. Instead, energy prices, geopolitics and global risk appetite are likely to dominate. The forint also remains an important part of the National Bank of Hungary’s (NBH) inflation strategy, especially given the high degree of exchange rate pass-through. In this volatile environment, we expect rates to remain on hold for the next 9–12 months at 5.50%. Inflation may provide room for easing, but that room remains behind a closed door. Only a sustained and structural improvement in the risk environment is likely to provide the key.
EUR/HUF should remain contained within a 350-370 range: At the stronger end, 350 represents a natural line in the sand. A significant decline in Hungary’s risk premium could take the pair towards this level, but the accompanying dovish repricing would make a sustained break lower difficult. Markets are likely to bring forward expectations of rate cuts, reflecting the Monetary Council’s underlying dovish bias, a view we share. At the weaker end, the central bank’s readiness to use the exchange rate channel should limit any disorderly sell-off. A non-linear move towards or beyond 370 could trigger verbal intervention and, if necessary, direct market action. We see an actual policy rate hike as a last resort, with the central bank likely to reach for other interest rate tools, including the FX swap rate, before touching the base rate. Credible intervention does not always require the central bank to pull the trigger; if markets believe the threat, they will do much of the heavy lifting themselves.
Domestic factors should keep the forint on the stronger side: Without a singular defining event, markets will closely monitor monthly budget execution, inflation developments, and progress in fiscal consolidation. Actual EU-fund inflows, an expected return of the current account to surplus and the possibility of positive sovereign rating actions should keep the forint closer to the stronger end of its range. A gradual grind lower in EUR/HUF could even bring 350 into view at moments of peak optimism. However, such strength would probably be followed by monetary easing, preventing a lasting appreciation beyond that level. We therefore see the forint primarily as a tactical market within a longer-term constructive story, supported by Hungary’s potential path towards ERM II entry at the start of 2029.
EUR/CZK: Koruna holds up well in tough times
This is not a hiking cycle: The Czech National Bank (CNB) increased the policy rate to 4% in two steps yet stressed repeatedly that this doesn’t represent the onset of another hiking cycle. Moreover, the tone of the latest press conferences was relatively dovish, while the meeting with analysts revealed that the country’s dwindling economic performance is a growing concern for some board members. We saw few pushbacks against the idea that the equilibrium rate is likely higher than generally assumed. In turn, it seems we’re in the process of searching for the right spot in a world of growing uncertainty. A weaker koruna contributing to rising import prices will be one of the key factors that the CNB will watch when it comes to maintaining price stability over the next year, but interest rates should remain the policy tool of choice. Stable rates are the most likely outcome if our forecast for next year’s average inflation of 3.1% is right.
Constrained consumers: The second-round effects linked to the protracted Hormuz shock have started to materialise and will be felt in renewed annual increases in regulated prices and food prices. Large distributors are beginning to announce increases in energy and heating prices, while higher water charges will also play their part. With food prices also set to rise soon, there is little chance for any relaxation of the monetary policy stance, unless household consumption and economic performance prove weaker than expected. Indeed, disappointing real GDP figures could put a lid on a potential hiking spree. With real wage growth softening materially over the next year and borrowing costs rising, many households would be forced to reconsider their spending habits, especially when it comes to discretionary spending.
Koruna enjoys rate support: Still, we will continue to see a positive interest rate differential with the ECB in both nominal and real terms, which makes the koruna attractive. The domestic currency is set to remain stable in times of elevated uncertainty, while a gradual strengthening trajectory is likely once the global turmoil shows signs of settling down. Should oil prices recede further and remain lower for longer, we would see fresh wind in koruna’s sails, as this would prepare the ground for the Czech economic expansion to accelerate. Real convergence would get back on track, and the more pronounced outperformance relative to the eurozone’s real growth would once again work in koruna’s favour. Moreover, the CNB is free to raise rates as it pleases should domestic or imported inflation get out of hand; we have some doubts about whether the ECB has the same room for manoeuvre, as it must, like it or not, keep one eye on French bond yields.
EUR/RON: No big changes expected ahead
Monetary policy should remain the main near-term anchor for the leu: The National Bank of Romania (NBR) has continued to keep the policy rate at 6.50% throughout 2026, and our baseline remains for 50bp of easing in 2027, pending a smoother disinflation process. Weak activity and improving headline inflation would justify an early start, but sticky price pressures on the services front, potential episodes of political uncertainty and risk-off global events could delay the easing cycle. In this context, we think that liquidity management will remain an important part of NBR’s balancing act. The liquidity surplus fell sharply through October, from around RON20.8bn to RON4.9bn, supporting tighter money market conditions during the recent period of intense FX pressures. However, FX-implied yields have since retreated from an early-October peak to more manageable levels, broadly in line with their one-year average. Acute pressure on the currency seems to have eased since mid-October, although it’s not excluded that a smaller liquidity surplus going forward will continue to support monetary transmission and discourage renewed short positioning.
The domestic slowdown has yet to translate into a convincing correction of Romania’s external imbalance: Retail sales have been contracting for more than a year, reflecting weaker household demand, fiscal consolidation and elevated inflation. Nevertheless, the January-September trade deficit remained visibly elevated at 6.3% of GDP in 2026, only marginally narrower than 6.5% in 2025 and 6.7% in 2024 for the same period. The investment cycle has also sustained imports despite weaker consumption. In particular, the final push to complete RRF-funded infrastructure, transport, energy and healthcare projects has generated strong demand for imported machinery, equipment and intermediate inputs. We think that Romania’s potential growth currently sits at around 2.0%, but productive investment could lift it towards 2.4-2.7% in 2027-2029 through better infrastructure, connectivity and energy availability, which should favour the medium and long-term fundamentals for RON.
Our baseline is for further controlled depreciation in 2027, with fiscal credibility, political stability and capital flows as key factors to watch: Romania’s investment-grade rating preservation has provided some relief, but the cautious approach of markets with regards to fiscal implementation and the delivery of a credible medium-term consolidation plan remains in place. In this context, uncertainties over Romania’s capacity to absorb the remaining €6.4bn of RRF funds represents an additional short-term risk. Delays or lower-than-expected absorption would place greater pressure on domestic and market-based funding. We think that the NBR will continue to maintain a rather firm grip on the currency, discouraging one-sided positioning. We expect EUR/RON to remain around 5.35 by end-2026 and move gradually towards 5.45 by end-2027. Renewed episodes of political instability, fiscal slippage or weaker RRF absorption could produce a faster depreciation.
EUR/RSD: Stability is likely to prevail
Active FX management should remain the main anchor for the dinar: The National Bank of Serbia (NBS) surprised with a 25bp hike to 6.0% at the November meeting, seeking to contain second-round inflation effects from persistently high energy prices, while also leaning against the recent depreciation pressure on the dinar. Our baseline outlook forecasts no further hikes at this stage, and we expect 50bp of rate cuts in 2027 (likely through the second half of the year), taking the policy rate to 5.50% by end-2027. Nevertheless, we think that the balance tilts more towards upside risks for rates, rather than to the downside. Currency stability has been a key policy feature this year and is likely set to remain an integral part of the policy framework ahead; the NBS sold €475m between January and September, including substantial intervention in September, when it sold €380m as energy-related FX demand increased. In any case, reserves remain comfortable, giving the central bank ample capacity to contain volatility moving forwards.
A stronger domestic economy should support the dinar, although fiscal stimulus and investment-related imports create external and inflationary trade-offs: Serbia’s GDP expanded by 4.0% year-on-year in 3Q26, accelerating from 3.8% in the second quarter and 3.2% in the first. Private consumption, a resilient labour market and the investment programme ahead of EXPO 2027 should continue to support activity ahead. However, the more expansionary fiscal stance, infrastructure spending and the import-intensive nature of the investment cycle could also act as catalysts for slightly stronger price pressures and trade deficits in the near term. That said, at around 43% of GDP, public debt remains manageable, while Serbia’s macro fundamentals continue to remain robust.
We expect EUR/RSD to remain broadly stable around 117.4-117.5 through 2027, although domestic politics and the unresolved NIS transaction present near-term risks: The Student List won the 25 October parliamentary election, ending the previous governing bloc’s longstanding dominance. While the result could support institutional reform and closer EU alignment, uncertainty around the political transition and future policy direction, alongside energy-related FX demand, likely contributed to the dinar’s modest weakening towards 117.6. Meanwhile, 11 December is the target for completing negotiations under which Hungarian oil group MOL would acquire the Russian-controlled stake in Serbian oil company NIS, although a final purchase agreement and regulatory approvals remain outstanding. With substantial reserves and a demonstrated commitment to FX stability, the NBS should be able to absorb further temporary pressures and keep the currency close to its desired range.
USD/UAH: Orderly hryvnia depreciation
Gradual UAH depreciation ahead: The hryvnia has weakened to record lows against the US dollar. Even so, we expect further gradual depreciation. Pressure stems from a firmer dollar on the back of a hawkish Fed and renewed tension in the Middle East as well as intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's economy. The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) continues its strategy of "managed flexibility": it tolerates an orderly slide but intervenes heavily in the FX market to prevent disorderly moves. Monetary policy has turned tighter, with a series of rate hikes since the summer reaching 150bp in total accompanied by guidance that rates will stay high well into 2027, as inflation has turned into double-digit territory recently.
FX reserves have declined: External financing remains the key anchor for the hryvnia. However, international reserves have fallen markedly from their record highs earlier in the year, as FX interventions and debt service outpaced inflows. On one hand, disbursements under the EU's Ukraine Support Loan have lagged behind plans because of delays in agreed reforms, and Brussels has made further funding conditional on their implementation. On the other hand, according to NBU data, the FX interventions at the end of October were the highest in history.
Focus on peace negotiations: The macroeconomic outlook has deteriorated significantly because of the Russian war, but direct technical peace talks between Ukraine and Russia with US participation offer some hope of an end to the war. Intensified attacks on industry, energy and logistics, together with the blockade of seaports, have pushed the economy back into contraction this year, while renewed inflationary pressure is eroding real incomes. Labour shortages linked to mobilisation and rising production costs continue to weigh on competitiveness, and any recovery in 2027 is likely to be slow. Against this backdrop, we expect USD/UAH to drift gradually higher, towards the 46.0 area in the coming months, at a pace the NBU appears willing to accept as long as it remains orderly. Timely EU and IMF disbursements are the main upside factor, while a ceasefire with Russia, which would change the picture materially, does not look imminent despite intensified US diplomatic efforts.
USD/KZT: Carry can cushion external risks
High real rates should survive NBK easing cycle: The tenge enters 2027 with monetary policy still favouring portfolio inflows. The National Bank of the Republic of Kazakhstan (NBK) started cutting rates in 2026 to 15.75% currently, as inflation moderated to 9.2% YoY and the currency strengthened, but the policy stance remained cautious, with cuts lagging the actual CPI slowdown. We expect the easing cycle to remain gradual, leaving real rates high by regional and EM standards. This matters increasingly for KZT as foreign participation in Kazakhstan's local debt has been a key driver of the tenge's strength this year. The main risk to our constructive view would be a faster easing cycle than we expect, particularly if inflation proves stickier and reduces the real-rate cushion. Conversely, sustained disinflation accompanied by cautious rate cuts should preserve attractive carry and keep monetary policy an important source of support for KZT.
Capital flows are a new strength, but also a new sensitivity: One of the biggest changes in the KZT story over the last 12 months has been the growing role of foreign portfolio flows. Progress towards Euroclear connectivity, positive sovereign rating momentum, increased domestic debt issuance and high real yields have helped attract foreign investors into KZT government bonds. At the same time, regular state-related FX sales have fallen sharply. This makes the tenge more market-driven, but also more exposed to changes in global rates and risk appetite. After its strong rally, we see limited room for another large appreciation. However, downside risks are also cushioned: a $2.2bn backlog of National Fund-related FX sales accumulated between June and October gives the authorities a potentially significant supply buffer should private inflows reverse. We therefore expect KZT to remain resilient in 2027 even if global portfolio flows become less supportive.
Resilience does not equal structural appreciation: Higher core yields or a broader global risk-off episode, AI-led or otherwise, could weaken foreign demand for KZT assets and put pressure on the currency. This is increasingly relevant as carry-driven flows become a bigger part of the KZT story. But we would not expect an indiscriminate sell-off; still-high real rates and the accumulated backlog of state FX sales provide meaningful buffers against a reversal in private inflows, while the role of oil should not be overestimated as export constraints, growing imports and large dividend outflows prevented the tenge from benefitting materially from the recent oil price rally. Our constructive 2027 view should therefore not be confused with a structurally bullish view on KZT. Kazakhstan's persistent current account deficit remains consistent with gradual depreciation over the longer term. For 2027, however, we expect domestic buffers to keep any depreciation contained even under a less supportive global backdrop.
USD/UZS: Domestic buffers should keep the soum resilient
High real rates are here to stay: Uzbekistan enters 2027 with monetary policy providing a substantial buffer against global volatility. The Central Bank of Uzbekistan (CBU) kept its policy rate at 14.00% in November and turned more cautious on inflation, raising its year-end forecast to around 7% amid strong domestic demand, utility tariff increases and external food and energy risks. This makes near-term easing unlikely, but we still see scope for cautious cuts in 2027 if fiscal restraint continues and inflation pressures subside. Crucially for the soum, easing should not require sacrificing the sizeable real-rate cushion. This should help retain carry support even if global rates remain elevated. The main risk would be a combination of sticky inflation and weaker FX, which would leave the central bank with less room to cut and potentially require real rates to remain higher for longer.
Gold export backlog provides an additional buffer if capital flows weaken: The soum's resilience this year is particularly notable because it has received relatively little help from Uzbekistan's traditional source of FX support. Only 18 tonnes of gold were exported in January-September 2026, compared with 85 tonnes during the same period of 2025, despite much stronger gold prices. Instead, the soum's strength appears to have been driven largely by capital inflows. That creates both a vulnerability and a potential buffer for 2027. Higher global yields or a broader risk-off episode could weaken carry-driven flows, but a recovery in physical gold shipments towards Uzbekistan's historical 80-120 tonne annual range would bring additional FX supply into the market. Combined with still-high real rates and continued reform-related capital inflows, this should limit the soum's vulnerability to a deterioration in global sentiment.
It is too early to consider the old depreciation trend defeated: We therefore remain constructive on UZS for 2027, but like KZT, would distinguish resilience from a permanently stronger currency. Continued fiscal consolidation is helpful, with the deficit having fallen from 4.7% of GDP in 2023 to below 2% currently, but Uzbekistan continues to run twin deficits and somewhat elevated inflation risks. Higher core yields or a global risk-off episode could still weaken carry support and put depreciation pressure on UZS, although high real rates and catch-up gold exports provide meaningful buffers against a large adjustment. Over the longer term, we would therefore remain cautious about extrapolating recent soum strength. For 2027, however, the combination of restrictive real rates, fiscal restraint and potentially stronger gold-related FX inflows should keep depreciation contained even under a less supportive global backdrop.
USD/TRY: Controlled lira depreciation to continue
Inflation path delayed in 2027: October inflation in Turkey came in slightly above expectations, interrupting the recent downtrend. Even so, we see annual inflation finishing the year below 30%. In the near term, uncertainty around oil prices remains a key risk to the outlook. Prolonged US-Iran tensions could quickly intensify price pressures, particularly as the sliding scale mechanism continues to unwind. The latest Medium-Term Programme raised the 2027 forecast to 21%, up from 9% in the previous plan. Although revised higher, this projection remains optimistic compared with the 23.3% expectation reflected in the Market Participants Survey. The upward adjustment mainly reflects both the carry-over effect of stronger-than-anticipated inflation this year on next year’s starting point and the influence of global economic conditions. Overall, the new forecast suggests that the disinflation process under the stabilisation programme launched in mid-2023 has been pushed further out. We forecast 26% next year, with risks to the upside.
CBT signals gradual easing: In its latest MPC statement, the Central Bank of Turkey (CBT) adjusted its language, shifting attention from “monetary policy decisions” to the scale and timing of future policy actions. This change suggests that, unless the factors behind the current easing cycle change materially, the Bank is likely to continue lowering rates in December. From this perspective, October inflation is unlikely to significantly alter the policy outlook. The main risks for policy remain developments in the Middle East and any deterioration in the disinflation trend. At the same time, the Bank is expected to keep a close watch on domestic demand, international reserve dynamics, and depositor behaviour when assessing future policy moves. Maintaining sufficiently attractive real interest rates is likely to remain important in limiting pressure on foreign exchange reserves. Against this backdrop, we continue to expect the easing cycle to move forward gradually, with the policy rate reaching 30% by end-2027.
Reserve accumulation resumes in early November: Investment fund volatility has had only a limited effect on dollarisation across deposits and mutual funds, although lira-denominated funds experienced outflows as some investors appeared to reduce money market fund positions. At the same time, growth in TRY deposits and repo accounts indicates that dollarization pressures have remained contained. After accumulating more than $30bn through net foreign exchange purchases between June and August, the CBT saw both its gross reserves and net FX position excluding swaps decline in September and October, largely reflecting turbulence in investment funds. However, the Bank’s net FX position rose sharply in early November, pointing to a return of non-resident inflows alongside subdued foreign currency demand from residents. Additionally, although the CBT increased the pace of FX depreciation lately, this appears to be a technical adjustment rather than a change in exchange rate policy, a stance likely to persist ahead of the 2028 election period.
USD/ZAR: Hawkish SARB and key reforms in focus
South African Reserve Bank stays hawkish: Having adopted a 3% inflation target in 2025, the SARB has already hiked twice this year. With fuel prices looking like they will stay high, the SARB is expecting headline inflation to stay above 5% and is also concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored. The risk of higher food prices from El Niño drought conditions later this year is not helping either. But even with growth contracting in the second quarter, the SARB is clearly taking no chances with inflation. The market now expects another 75bp of tightening (to 8.00%) over the next 12 months and policy to remain firmly in restrictive territory. High implied yields and relatively (by the rand’s standards) low volatility have made the rand one of the better EMFX performers this year.
2027 will be a big year for reforms: Increasingly, we are hearing about the need for legislated reforms to be implemented. These largely focus on the energy and freight sectors. On the former, Eskom’s ability to avoid further load-shedding, increase generation, improve its finances and integrate the private sector will be key. On the latter, whether 11 private train companies can start using Transnet infrastructure to dramatically increase freight volumes will be a key test. The good news is that the Government for National Unity (GNU) seems to be finding a way through thorny issues – e.g., finally passing the 2025 budget – and the next national elections are not due until 2029. Consensus currently expects South African growth in the 1.5-2.0% area.
Local assets have withstood external pressure well: Local asset markets seem to have withstood the strong dollar and the US Treasury sell-off relatively well. One-month USD/ZAR traded option prices have been happy to trade at low, sub-10% levels since the summer. And South Africa’s credit default swap remains relatively calm near +130bp, perhaps because of the country’s primary fiscal surplus and a more manageable current account deficit of less than 2% of GDP. Additionally, despite the flows into South Africa last year after the SARB adopted the 3% inflation target, foreigners only hold 25% of available South African government bonds. This compares with a peak of 43% back in 2018. Overall, we expect a hawkish SARB to limit the rand’s downside, while some improvement in the external environment next year, plus some progress on implementing key reforms, should allow the rand to continue to perform well.
USD/ILS: Bank of Israel gets what it wants
Bank of Israel fights shekel strength: Having traded as low as 2.80 in late May, USD/ILS looks to be heading into year-end well above 3.00. Yes, the strong dollar has played a role here, but so has the Bank of Israel (BoI). This year, it has cut rates by 100bp to 3.25% and also intervened to buy USD/ILS back in May. The BoI’s dovish position has been justified by CPI continuing to surprise on the downside. CPI has been below the middle of the BoI’s target range (1-3%) all year. Yet we suspect the BoI is more worried about the strong shekel from a growth perspective. Here, the real, trade-weighted shekel remains 30% above its 20-year average and will prove to be a headwind to Israeli exporters. While Washington may want trading partners to step back from FX intervention against local currency strength, it may see Israel as a special case.
Shekel joined at the hip with tech: Part of the recent shekel weakness may reflect weakness in the US tech sector. Strength there normally helps the shekel via two channels: investment flows and hedging. On the former, a tougher IPO environment may well be weighing on flows into Israel. During good times, these flows can be worth as much as $5bn per quarter through the Israeli current account. On the latter, a big fall in tech can see Israeli investors reduce their hedges on falling overseas portfolios. For example, in the second quarter, Israeli pension funds and insurers sold $18bn of FX against the shekel as they increased FX hedges on booming tech portfolios. The reverse may be happening now and leaves the shekel a little vulnerable if the US tech story has further to correct.
Good-quality credit and current account surplus help: While the BoI may not want USD/ILS to go too much below 3.00, that does not mean USD/ILS needs to rally a lot either. Israel is seen as a solid A- sovereign credit and has very strong FX reserve coverage of short-term debt and imports. Its budget deficit of 4-5% of GDP is seen as manageable, and its perennial current account surplus of 1-2% of GDP normally provides good natural demand for the shekel. We suspect there will be good interest for the shekel over the coming months in the 3.20/3.40 area. Any improvement in geopolitics would also be a positive for the shekel both on the budgetary and labour market sides, with scarce labour resources curtailing Israel’s potential growth rate.

articles.title: As good as it gets for the dollar: 3 calls for FX
articles.author: Chris Turner
articles.fulltext:
The dollar should stay supported by strong US growth, high inflation and a Fed threatening to tighten before weakening next spring as inflation falls. An AI correction looms large, and what about attractive overseas growth drawing funds away from the dollar?
How to read our three calls for 2027
ING’s base call: Dollar stays supported until next spring
Our base call assumes that the Federal Reserve stays hawkish in the first quarter, as decent US growth and above-3% inflation keep money markets pricing in the threat of an extended tightening cycle. That turns in the second quarter, when energy-driven base effects drop out of headline inflation and a return to the Fed’s 2% inflation target sees short-dated US rates move meaningfully lower.
That timing also suits events in Europe. French budgetary politics look set to keep a risk premium in the euro ahead of April's elections. We therefore see EUR/USD trading offered in a 1.10-15 range over the next four to five months. From the second quarter, however, softer US rates, moderating energy prices and clarity on French politics could trigger a gentle recovery in EUR/USD towards 1.18 by year-end 2027.
Our risky call: AI bust
Energy and AI have been the dominant global macro drivers this year and could well shape FX markets again in 2027. An AI bust is not the base case, but if it occurred, it would lead to a lower dollar. The IMF estimates the dollar could fall 6% under such a scenario.
The nature of the dollar decline could be erratic, however. If the functioning of the financial system were to come into question, such as dollar liquidity drying up again, the dollar could first rally. But the inevitable Fed support measures to address liquidity needs and the likely large rate cuts would ultimately push the dollar a lot lower.
Our bold call: Overseas growth surprises positively
EUR/USD rallied sharply in 2017 when Dutch and French elections saw euro-sceptic parties failing to advance. Having toned down her views on France leaving the euro, a decisive victory by Marine Le Pen in April and greater budget clarity could reassure markets. If eurozone growth continues to defy energy and political headwinds, a rotation to European assets could be the surprise package for EUR/USD.
We’re also watching Japan for signs that it could follow South Korea’s lead and deliver stronger growth. There, chip exports have benefited the broader economy and the Bank of Korea revised up this year’s GDP forecast to 3.3%, from 1.8% at the start of 2026. Japan supplies the manufacturing equipment and materials for chip production. Broader benefits to the economy from loose fiscal policy could see upside surprises to Japanese growth, tighter Bank of Japan policy and a much weaker USD/JPY.

articles.title: Rates on the brink: 3 calls for 2027
articles.author: Padhraic Garvey, CFA
articles.fulltext:
Our base call sees yields rising to 5.25-5.5% before easing to 4.5-4.75% as inflation cools. Our risky call has US 10-year yields at 6% and German yields at 4%, while our bold call sees systemic stress triggering de facto yield curve control
How to read our three calls for 2027
ING's base call: Renewed upward pressure on long rates, but it ultimately wanes
We expect upward pressure on Treasury yields to persist into early 2027, with AI-driven productivity growth, large fiscal deficits and sticky inflation potentially pushing the 10-year towards 5.25-5.50%. The turn should come later as inflation softens and Fed easing expectations return, pulling yields towards 4.50-4.75%. Inflation remains the key threat heading into 2027.
For euro rates, second-round inflation concerns could push 10yr swaps above 4%, but we think markets have gone too far in pricing an ECB terminal rate above 3%. Our end-2027 baseline remains 2.5%, while downside for longer-dated rates looks more limited. AI is an upside risk.
France remains the focus in sovereign spreads, with elevated risk premia likely into the elections and some widening elsewhere. But it could also offer the biggest subsequent rally: once the elections pass, receding fears of another eurozone crisis should leave considerable room for French spreads to retrace.
Our risky call: Long tenor rates just keep on rising through 2027
There are three credible routes to 6% Treasuries and 4% Bunds.
First, inflation. Another energy shock, El Niño disruption or simply more persistent underlying inflation could keep central banks tighter for longer, pushing yields higher across the curve.
Second, AI. A genuine economy-wide productivity boom could lift potential growth and equilibrium real rates. The dot-com era offers a precedent: strong US growth helped push 10-year Treasury yields above 6% despite relatively benign inflation expectations. A comparable AI-driven productivity shock could have a similar effect.
Third, fiscal risk. A sharp deterioration in confidence over US and European fiscal trajectories could generate significant government-bond underperformance versus swaps. In this scenario, the move toward 6% and 4% would reflect rising fiscal and term premia rather than expectations of tighter monetary policy.
Our bold call: Long tenor rates are forced to lurch lower on official sector intervention
At the extreme, policymakers could decide that rising bond yields pose an unacceptable threat to financial stability. In the eurozone, that could mean the ECB overlooking fiscal recklessness and prioritising the stability of the system and the euro. Existing programmes leave it with considerable firepower to contain yields and fragmentation.
The US has its own levers. The Treasury could cut long-end issuance and shift financing towards the front end, while the Fed could keep the funds rate sufficiently low to preserve cheap funding and counter market stress. Taken to its extreme, renewed Fed bond buying could push the desired yield structure into place.
The paradox is that policies designed to protect the system could generate even greater systemic risk through de facto yield curve control. For the US, the aim would be a generic funding rate below 4%, ideally around 3.5%. For the eurozone, the result would likely be yield containment, with German yields ultimately trading broadly in line with Treasuries.
